newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts welcome Sweden boost in T-bill liquidity.
newsitem.headline: Analysts welcome Sweden boost in T-bill liquidity.

text.p: The Swedish National Debt Office's moves to increase liquidity in the Treasury bill market was in line with market makers' wishes, a trader told Reuters on Tuesday.
"Everybody was allowed to express an opinion and this is in principle the opinion many had," he said.

To combine a lower T-bill stock with strong liquidity in the market, the National Debt Office on Tuesday announced it would start reducing the number of T-bill maturities to eight from 12 and concentrate volumes to maturities on the so-called International Money Market (IMM) days.
At the same time, a new repurchase, repo, facility for new loans will be set up for market makers. This facility, including the volume issued, will total 10 billion crowns.

For example, if six billion crowns are issued in T-bills, four billion remains for the repurchase facility which allows the 14 market makers in Sweden to buy another 285 million crowns of T-bills each, which they then have to sell back to the debt office.
Analysts think these measures are a fairly logical way to keep liquidity in the T-bill market and maintain good price development.
"If you want to keep up index-linked bonds and benchmark bond markets, it will create a problem on the T-bill side," said Knut Hallberg, economist at banking group Swedbank.
"It is hard to keep full issue volumes in all three as the National Debt Office does not have to borrow so much (anymore)."
On Tuesday, the National Debt Office cut its borrowing requirement forecast to 20-30 billion crowns for 1997, from 25-35 million.
The Debt Office's new issue model contains six T-bill loans with maturities between one and six months and two loans with maturities between seven and 12 months.
"Some market makers wanted to reduce the number of T-bill maturities to four, while others wanted to keep the current number," a trader said. "This is a compromise."
The sensitive part is the longer end of the T-bill curve where there are fewer maturities. This makes it more difficult to diversify, the trader said.
On the other hand, the short end of the bond market will benefit from this situation.
"This is advantageous for the three-year bond (no 1028) and the shorter real estate bonds, but also for commercial paper programs," said Peter Lindquist, economist at HSBC Midland.
The National Debt Office intends to see that the longer T-bills quickly get volumes of 25 billion crowns at the current borrowing requirement level.
"For December and March T-bills, the outlook is favourable," a trader said. "But later it could take some time to fill them. The repo facility could underpin liquidity if there is a good price."
